              [14, TagBody] <div class="vector-body-before-content">\\n <div class="mw-indicators">\\n </div>\\n\\n <div id="siteSub" class="noprint">From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia</div>\\n </div>\\n <div id="contentSub"><div id="mw-content-subtitle"></div></div>\\n \\n \\n <div id="mw-content-text" class="mw-body-content"><div class="mw-content-ltr mw-parser-output" lang="en" dir="ltr"><div class="shortdescription nomobile noexcerpt noprint searchaux" style="display:none">Method of providing unique elements and attributes in an XML document</div>\\n<p><b>XML namespaces</b> are used for providing uniquely named <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_element" title="Data element">elements</a> and attributes in an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XML" title="XML">XML</a> document. They are defined in a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web_Consortium" title="World Wide Web Consortium">W3C recommendation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-timelinehistory_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-timelinehistory-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> An XML instance may contain element or attribute names from more than one XML vocabulary. If each vocabulary is given a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namespace" title="Namespace">namespace</a>, the ambiguity between identically named elements or attributes can be resolved.\\n</p><p>A simple example would be to consider an XML instance that \\ncontained references to a customer and an ordered product. Both the \\ncustomer element and the product element could have a child element \\nnamed <b>id</b>. References to the <b>id</b> element would therefore be ambiguous; placing them in different namespaces would remove the ambiguity.\\n</p>\\n<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc">\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespace_names">Namespace names</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: Namespace names"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>A <i>namespace name</i> is a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_identifier" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource identifier">uniform resource identifier</a>\\n (URI). Typically, the URI chosen for the namespace of a given XML \\nvocabulary describes a resource under the control of the author or \\norganization defining the vocabulary, such as a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_locator" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource locator">URL</a>\\n for the author's Web server. However, the namespace specification does \\nnot require nor suggest that the namespace URI be used to retrieve \\ninformation; it is simply treated by an XML parser as a string. For \\nexample, the document at <a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a> itself does not contain any code. It simply describes the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XHTML" title="XHTML">XHTML</a>\\n namespace to human readers. Using a URI (such as \\n"http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml") to identify a namespace, rather than a \\nsimple string (such as "xhtml"), reduces the probability of different \\nnamespaces using duplicate identifiers.\\n</p><p>Although the term <i>namespace URI</i> is widespread, the W3C Recommendation refers to it as the <i>namespace name</i>.\\n The specification is not entirely prescriptive about the precise rules \\nfor namespace names (it does not explicitly say that parsers must reject\\n documents where the namespace name is not a valid <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Resource_Identifier" title="Uniform Resource Identifier">Uniform Resource Identifier</a>),\\n and many XML parsers allow any character string to be used. In version \\n1.1 of the recommendation, the namespace name becomes an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationalized_Resource_Identifier" title="Internationalized Resource Identifier">Internationalized Resource Identifier</a>, which licenses the use of non-ASCII characters that in practice were already accepted by nearly all XML software. The term <i>namespace URI</i> persists, however, not only in popular usage, but also in many other specifications from W3C and elsewhere.\\n</p><p>Following publication of the Namespaces recommendation, there was\\n an intensive debate about how a relative URI should be handled, with \\nsome intensely arguing that it should simply be treated as a character \\nstring, and others arguing with conviction that it should be turned into\\n an absolute URI by resolving it against the base URI of the document.<sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The result of the debate was a ruling from W3C that relative URIs were deprecated.<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>\\n</p><p>The use of URIs taking the form of URLs in the http scheme (such as <i><a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a></i>)\\n is common, despite the absence of any formal relationship with the HTTP\\n protocol. The Namespaces specification does not say what should happen \\nif such a URL is dereferenced (that is, if software attempts to retrieve\\n a document from this location). One convention adopted by some users is\\n to place an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RDDL" class="mw-redirect" title="RDDL">RDDL</a> document at the location.<sup id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In general, however, users should assume that the namespace URI is simply a name, not the address of a document on the Web.\\n</p>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespace_declaration">Namespace declaration</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: Namespace declaration"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>An XML namespace is declared using the reserved XML attribute <code>xmlns</code> or <code>xmlns:<i>prefix</i></code>, the value of which must be a valid <a href="#Namespace_names">namespace name</a>.\\n</p><p>For example, the following declaration maps the "xhtml:" prefix to the XHTML namespace:\\n</p>\\n<pre>xmlns:xhtml="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"</pre>\\n<p>Any element or attribute whose name starts with the prefix "xhtml:" \\nis considered to be in the XHTML namespace, if it or an ancestor has the\\n above namespace declaration.\\n</p><p>It is also possible to declare a default namespace. For example:\\n</p>\\n<pre>xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"</pre>\\n<p>In this case, any element without a namespace prefix is considered to\\n be in the XHTML namespace, if it or an ancestor has the above default \\nnamespace declaration.\\n</p><p>If there is no default namespace declaration in scope, the namespace name has no value.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In that case, an element without an explicit namespace prefix is considered not to be in any namespace.\\n</p><p>Attributes are never subject to the default namespace. An \\nattribute without an explicit namespace prefix is considered not to be \\nin any namespace.\\n</p>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespaces_in_APIs_and_XML_object_models">Namespaces in APIs and XML object models</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Namespaces in APIs and XML object models"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>Different specifications have taken different approaches on how namespace information is presented to applications.\\n</p><p>Nearly all programming models allow the name of an element or \\nattribute node to be retrieved as a three-part name: the local name, the\\n namespace prefix, and the namespace URI. Applications should avoid \\nattaching any significance to the choice of prefix, but the information \\nis provided because it can be helpful to human readers. Names are \\nconsidered equal if the namespace URI and local name match.\\n</p><p>In addition, most models provide some way of determining which \\nnamespaces have been declared for a given element. This information is \\nneeded because some XML vocabularies allow qualified names (containing \\nnamespace prefixes) to appear in the content of elements or attributes, \\nas well as in their names. There are three main ways this information \\ncan be provided:\\n</p>\\n<ul><li>As attribute nodes named "xmlns" or "xmlns:xxx", exactly as the \\nnamespaces are written in the source XML document. This is the model \\npresented by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Document_Object_Model" title="Document Object Model">DOM</a>.</li>\\n<li>As namespace declarations: distinguished from attributes, but \\ncorresponding one-to-one with the relevant attributes in the source XML \\ndocument. This is the model presented by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JDOM" title="JDOM">JDOM</a>.</li>\\n<li>As in-scope namespace bindings: in this model, the application is \\nable to determine which namespaces are in scope for any given element, \\nbut is not able to determine which elements contain the actual \\ndeclarations. This is the model used in <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XPath" title="XPath">XPath</a>, <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XSLT" title="XSLT">XSLT</a>, and <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XQuery" title="XQuery">XQuery</a>.</li></ul>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="See_also">See also</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=4" title="Edit section: See also"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<ul><li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namespace" title="Namespace">Namespace</a></li></ul>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2                [15, Tag] <div id="mw-content-text" class="mw-body-content"><div class="mw-content-ltr mw-parser-output" lang="en" dir="ltr"><div class="shortdescription nomobile noexcerpt noprint searchaux" style="display:none">Method of providing unique elements and attributes in an XML document</div>\\n<p><b>XML namespaces</b> are used for providing uniquely named <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_element" title="Data element">elements</a> and attributes in an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XML" title="XML">XML</a> document. They are defined in a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web_Consortium" title="World Wide Web Consortium">W3C recommendation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-timelinehistory_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-timelinehistory-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> An XML instance may contain element or attribute names from more than one XML vocabulary. If each vocabulary is given a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namespace" title="Namespace">namespace</a>, the ambiguity between identically named elements or attributes can be resolved.\\n</p><p>A simple example would be to consider an XML instance that \\ncontained references to a customer and an ordered product. Both the \\ncustomer element and the product element could have a child element \\nnamed <b>id</b>. References to the <b>id</b> element would therefore be ambiguous; placing them in different namespaces would remove the ambiguity.\\n</p>\\n<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc">\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespace_names">Namespace names</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: Namespace names"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>A <i>namespace name</i> is a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_identifier" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource identifier">uniform resource identifier</a>\\n (URI). Typically, the URI chosen for the namespace of a given XML \\nvocabulary describes a resource under the control of the author or \\norganization defining the vocabulary, such as a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_locator" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource locator">URL</a>\\n for the author's Web server. However, the namespace specification does \\nnot require nor suggest that the namespace URI be used to retrieve \\ninformation; it is simply treated by an XML parser as a string. For \\nexample, the document at <a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a> itself does not contain any code. It simply describes the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XHTML" title="XHTML">XHTML</a>\\n namespace to human readers. Using a URI (such as \\n"http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml") to identify a namespace, rather than a \\nsimple string (such as "xhtml"), reduces the probability of different \\nnamespaces using duplicate identifiers.\\n</p><p>Although the term <i>namespace URI</i> is widespread, the W3C Recommendation refers to it as the <i>namespace name</i>.\\n The specification is not entirely prescriptive about the precise rules \\nfor namespace names (it does not explicitly say that parsers must reject\\n documents where the namespace name is not a valid <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Resource_Identifier" title="Uniform Resource Identifier">Uniform Resource Identifier</a>),\\n and many XML parsers allow any character string to be used. In version \\n1.1 of the recommendation, the namespace name becomes an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationalized_Resource_Identifier" title="Internationalized Resource Identifier">Internationalized Resource Identifier</a>, which licenses the use of non-ASCII characters that in practice were already accepted by nearly all XML software. The term <i>namespace URI</i> persists, however, not only in popular usage, but also in many other specifications from W3C and elsewhere.\\n</p><p>Following publication of the Namespaces recommendation, there was\\n an intensive debate about how a relative URI should be handled, with \\nsome intensely arguing that it should simply be treated as a character \\nstring, and others arguing with conviction that it should be turned into\\n an absolute URI by resolving it against the base URI of the document.<sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The result of the debate was a ruling from W3C that relative URIs were deprecated.<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>\\n</p><p>The use of URIs taking the form of URLs in the http scheme (such as <i><a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a></i>)\\n is common, despite the absence of any formal relationship with the HTTP\\n protocol. The Namespaces specification does not say what should happen \\nif such a URL is dereferenced (that is, if software attempts to retrieve\\n a document from this location). One convention adopted by some users is\\n to place an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RDDL" class="mw-redirect" title="RDDL">RDDL</a> document at the location.<sup id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In general, however, users should assume that the namespace URI is simply a name, not the address of a document on the Web.\\n</p>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespace_declaration">Namespace declaration</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: Namespace declaration"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>An XML namespace is declared using the reserved XML attribute <code>xmlns</code> or <code>xmlns:<i>prefix</i></code>, the value of which must be a valid <a href="#Namespace_names">namespace name</a>.\\n</p><p>For example, the following declaration maps the "xhtml:" prefix to the XHTML namespace:\\n</p>\\n<pre>xmlns:xhtml="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"</pre>\\n<p>Any element or attribute whose name starts with the prefix "xhtml:" \\nis considered to be in the XHTML namespace, if it or an ancestor has the\\n above namespace declaration.\\n</p><p>It is also possible to declare a default namespace. For example:\\n</p>\\n<pre>xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"</pre>\\n<p>In this case, any element without a namespace prefix is considered to\\n be in the XHTML namespace, if it or an ancestor has the above default \\nnamespace declaration.\\n</p><p>If there is no default namespace declaration in scope, the namespace name has no value.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In that case, an element without an explicit namespace prefix is considered not to be in any namespace.\\n</p><p>Attributes are never subject to the default namespace. An \\nattribute without an explicit namespace prefix is considered not to be \\nin any namespace.\\n</p>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespaces_in_APIs_and_XML_object_models">Namespaces in APIs and XML object models</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Namespaces in APIs and XML object models"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>Different specifications have taken different approaches on how namespace information is presented to applications.\\n</p><p>Nearly all programming models allow the name of an element or \\nattribute node to be retrieved as a three-part name: the local name, the\\n namespace prefix, and the namespace URI. Applications should avoid \\nattaching any significance to the choice of prefix, but the information \\nis provided because it can be helpful to human readers. Names are \\nconsidered equal if the namespace URI and local name match.\\n</p><p>In addition, most models provide some way of determining which \\nnamespaces have been declared for a given element. This information is \\nneeded because some XML vocabularies allow qualified names (containing \\nnamespace prefixes) to appear in the content of elements or attributes, \\nas well as in their names. There are three main ways this information \\ncan be provided:\\n</p>\\n<ul><li>As attribute nodes named "xmlns" or "xmlns:xxx", exactly as the \\nnamespaces are written in the source XML document. This is the model \\npresented by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Document_Object_Model" title="Document Object Model">DOM</a>.</li>\\n<li>As namespace declarations: distinguished from attributes, but \\ncorresponding one-to-one with the relevant attributes in the source XML \\ndocument. This is the model presented by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JDOM" title="JDOM">JDOM</a>.</li>\\n<li>As in-scope namespace bindings: in this model, the application is \\nable to determine which namespaces are in scope for any given element, \\nbut is not able to determine which elements contain the actual \\ndeclarations. This is the model used in <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XPath" title="XPath">XPath</a>, <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XSLT" title="XSLT">XSLT</a>, and <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XQuery" title="XQuery">XQuery</a>.</li></ul>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="See_also">See also</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span                 [16, TagBody] <div class="mw-content-ltr mw-parser-output" lang="en" dir="ltr"><div class="shortdescription nomobile noexcerpt noprint searchaux" style="display:none">Method of providing unique elements and attributes in an XML document</div>\\n<p><b>XML namespaces</b> are used for providing uniquely named <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_element" title="Data element">elements</a> and attributes in an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XML" title="XML">XML</a> document. They are defined in a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web_Consortium" title="World Wide Web Consortium">W3C recommendation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-timelinehistory_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-timelinehistory-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> An XML instance may contain element or attribute names from more than one XML vocabulary. If each vocabulary is given a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namespace" title="Namespace">namespace</a>, the ambiguity between identically named elements or attributes can be resolved.\\n</p><p>A simple example would be to consider an XML instance that \\ncontained references to a customer and an ordered product. Both the \\ncustomer element and the product element could have a child element \\nnamed <b>id</b>. References to the <b>id</b> element would therefore be ambiguous; placing them in different namespaces would remove the ambiguity.\\n</p>\\n<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc">\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespace_names">Namespace names</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: Namespace names"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>A <i>namespace name</i> is a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_identifier" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource identifier">uniform resource identifier</a>\\n (URI). Typically, the URI chosen for the namespace of a given XML \\nvocabulary describes a resource under the control of the author or \\norganization defining the vocabulary, such as a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_locator" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource locator">URL</a>\\n for the author's Web server. However, the namespace specification does \\nnot require nor suggest that the namespace URI be used to retrieve \\ninformation; it is simply treated by an XML parser as a string. For \\nexample, the document at <a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a> itself does not contain any code. It simply describes the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XHTML" title="XHTML">XHTML</a>\\n namespace to human readers. Using a URI (such as \\n"http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml") to identify a namespace, rather than a \\nsimple string (such as "xhtml"), reduces the probability of different \\nnamespaces using duplicate identifiers.\\n</p><p>Although the term <i>namespace URI</i> is widespread, the W3C Recommendation refers to it as the <i>namespace name</i>.\\n The specification is not entirely prescriptive about the precise rules \\nfor namespace names (it does not explicitly say that parsers must reject\\n documents where the namespace name is not a valid <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Resource_Identifier" title="Uniform Resource Identifier">Uniform Resource Identifier</a>),\\n and many XML parsers allow any character string to be used. In version \\n1.1 of the recommendation, the namespace name becomes an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationalized_Resource_Identifier" title="Internationalized Resource Identifier">Internationalized Resource Identifier</a>, which licenses the use of non-ASCII characters that in practice were already accepted by nearly all XML software. The term <i>namespace URI</i> persists, however, not only in popular usage, but also in many other specifications from W3C and elsewhere.\\n</p><p>Following publication of the Namespaces recommendation, there was\\n an intensive debate about how a relative URI should be handled, with \\nsome intensely arguing that it should simply be treated as a character \\nstring, and others arguing with conviction that it should be turned into\\n an absolute URI by resolving it against the base URI of the document.<sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The result of the debate was a ruling from W3C that relative URIs were deprecated.<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>\\n</p><p>The use of URIs taking the form of URLs in the http scheme (such as <i><a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a></i>)\\n is common, despite the absence of any formal relationship with the HTTP\\n protocol. The Namespaces specification does not say what should happen \\nif such a URL is dereferenced (that is, if software attempts to retrieve\\n a document from this location). One convention adopted by some users is\\n to place an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RDDL" class="mw-redirect" title="RDDL">RDDL</a> document at the location.<sup id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In general, however, users should assume that the namespace URI is simply a name, not the address of a document on the Web.\\n</p>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespace_declaration">Namespace declaration</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: Namespace declaration"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>An XML namespace is declared using the reserved XML attribute <code>xmlns</code> or <code>xmlns:<i>prefix</i></code>, the value of which must be a valid <a href="#Namespace_names">namespace name</a>.\\n</p><p>For example, the following declaration maps the "xhtml:" prefix to the XHTML namespace:\\n</p>\\n<pre>xmlns:xhtml="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"</pre>\\n<p>Any element or attribute whose name starts with the prefix "xhtml:" \\nis considered to be in the XHTML namespace, if it or an ancestor has the\\n above namespace declaration.\\n</p><p>It is also possible to declare a default namespace. For example:\\n</p>\\n<pre>xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"</pre>\\n<p>In this case, any element without a namespace prefix is considered to\\n be in the XHTML namespace, if it or an ancestor has the above default \\nnamespace declaration.\\n</p><p>If there is no default namespace declaration in scope, the namespace name has no value.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In that case, an element without an explicit namespace prefix is considered not to be in any namespace.\\n</p><p>Attributes are never subject to the default namespace. An \\nattribute without an explicit namespace prefix is considered not to be \\nin any namespace.\\n</p>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespaces_in_APIs_and_XML_object_models">Namespaces in APIs and XML object models</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Namespaces in APIs and XML object models"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>Different specifications have taken different approaches on how namespace information is presented to applications.\\n</p><p>Nearly all programming models allow the name of an element or \\nattribute node to be retrieved as a three-part name: the local name, the\\n namespace prefix, and the namespace URI. Applications should avoid \\nattaching any significance to the choice of prefix, but the information \\nis provided because it can be helpful to human readers. Names are \\nconsidered equal if the namespace URI and local name match.\\n</p><p>In addition, most models provide some way of determining which \\nnamespaces have been declared for a given element. This information is \\nneeded because some XML vocabularies allow qualified names (containing \\nnamespace prefixes) to appear in the content of elements or attributes, \\nas well as in their names. There are three main ways this information \\ncan be provided:\\n</p>\\n<ul><li>As attribute nodes named "xmlns" or "xmlns:xxx", exactly as the \\nnamespaces are written in the source XML document. This is the model \\npresented by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Document_Object_Model" title="Document Object Model">DOM</a>.</li>\\n<li>As namespace declarations: distinguished from attributes, but \\ncorresponding one-to-one with the relevant attributes in the source XML \\ndocument. This is the model presented by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JDOM" title="JDOM">JDOM</a>.</li>\\n<li>As in-scope namespace bindings: in this model, the application is \\nable to determine which namespaces are in scope for any given element, \\nbut is not able to determine which elements contain the actual \\ndeclarations. This is the model used in <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XPath" title="XPath">XPath</a>, <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XSLT" title="XSLT">XSLT</a>, and <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XQuery" title="XQuery">XQuery</a>.</li></ul>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="See_also">See also</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=4" title="Edit section: See also"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<ul><li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namespace" title="Namespace">Namespace</a></li></ul>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2                  [17, Tag] <div class="mw-content-ltr mw-parser-output" lang="en" dir="ltr"><div class="shortdescription nomobile noexcerpt noprint searchaux" style="display:none">Method of providing unique elements and attributes in an XML document</div>\\n<p><b>XML namespaces</b> are used for providing uniquely named <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_element" title="Data element">elements</a> and attributes in an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XML" title="XML">XML</a> document. They are defined in a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web_Consortium" title="World Wide Web Consortium">W3C recommendation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-timelinehistory_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-timelinehistory-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> An XML instance may contain element or attribute names from more than one XML vocabulary. If each vocabulary is given a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namespace" title="Namespace">namespace</a>, the ambiguity between identically named elements or attributes can be resolved.\\n</p><p>A simple example would be to consider an XML instance that \\ncontained references to a customer and an ordered product. Both the \\ncustomer element and the product element could have a child element \\nnamed <b>id</b>. References to the <b>id</b> element would therefore be ambiguous; placing them in different namespaces would remove the ambiguity.\\n</p>\\n<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc">\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespace_names">Namespace names</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: Namespace names"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>A <i>namespace name</i> is a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_identifier" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource identifier">uniform resource identifier</a>\\n (URI). Typically, the URI chosen for the namespace of a given XML \\nvocabulary describes a resource under the control of the author or \\norganization defining the vocabulary, such as a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_locator" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource locator">URL</a>\\n for the author's Web server. However, the namespace specification does \\nnot require nor suggest that the namespace URI be used to retrieve \\ninformation; it is simply treated by an XML parser as a string. For \\nexample, the document at <a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a> itself does not contain any code. It simply describes the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XHTML" title="XHTML">XHTML</a>\\n namespace to human readers. Using a URI (such as \\n"http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml") to identify a namespace, rather than a \\nsimple string (such as "xhtml"), reduces the probability of different \\nnamespaces using duplicate identifiers.\\n</p><p>Although the term <i>namespace URI</i> is widespread, the W3C Recommendation refers to it as the <i>namespace name</i>.\\n The specification is not entirely prescriptive about the precise rules \\nfor namespace names (it does not explicitly say that parsers must reject\\n documents where the namespace name is not a valid <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Resource_Identifier" title="Uniform Resource Identifier">Uniform Resource Identifier</a>),\\n and many XML parsers allow any character string to be used. In version \\n1.1 of the recommendation, the namespace name becomes an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationalized_Resource_Identifier" title="Internationalized Resource Identifier">Internationalized Resource Identifier</a>, which licenses the use of non-ASCII characters that in practice were already accepted by nearly all XML software. The term <i>namespace URI</i> persists, however, not only in popular usage, but also in many other specifications from W3C and elsewhere.\\n</p><p>Following publication of the Namespaces recommendation, there was\\n an intensive debate about how a relative URI should be handled, with \\nsome intensely arguing that it should simply be treated as a character \\nstring, and others arguing with conviction that it should be turned into\\n an absolute URI by resolving it against the base URI of the document.<sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The result of the debate was a ruling from W3C that relative URIs were deprecated.<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>\\n</p><p>The use of URIs taking the form of URLs in the http scheme (such as <i><a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a></i>)\\n is common, despite the absence of any formal relationship with the HTTP\\n protocol. The Namespaces specification does not say what should happen \\nif such a URL is dereferenced (that is, if software attempts to retrieve\\n a document from this location). One convention adopted by some users is\\n to place an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RDDL" class="mw-redirect" title="RDDL">RDDL</a> document at the location.<sup id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In general, however, users should assume that the namespace URI is simply a name, not the address of a document on the Web.\\n</p>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespace_declaration">Namespace declaration</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: Namespace declaration"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>An XML namespace is declared using the reserved XML attribute <code>xmlns</code> or <code>xmlns:<i>prefix</i></code>, the value of which must be a valid <a href="#Namespace_names">namespace name</a>.\\n</p><p>For example, the following declaration maps the "xhtml:" prefix to the XHTML namespace:\\n</p>\\n<pre>xmlns:xhtml="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"</pre>\\n<p>Any element or attribute whose name starts with the prefix "xhtml:" \\nis considered to be in the XHTML namespace, if it or an ancestor has the\\n above namespace declaration.\\n</p><p>It is also possible to declare a default namespace. For example:\\n</p>\\n<pre>xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"</pre>\\n<p>In this case, any element without a namespace prefix is considered to\\n be in the XHTML namespace, if it or an ancestor has the above default \\nnamespace declaration.\\n</p><p>If there is no default namespace declaration in scope, the namespace name has no value.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In that case, an element without an explicit namespace prefix is considered not to be in any namespace.\\n</p><p>Attributes are never subject to the default namespace. An \\nattribute without an explicit namespace prefix is considered not to be \\nin any namespace.\\n</p>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespaces_in_APIs_and_XML_object_models">Namespaces in APIs and XML object models</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Namespaces in APIs and XML object models"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>Different specifications have taken different approaches on how namespace information is presented to applications.\\n</p><p>Nearly all programming models allow the name of an element or \\nattribute node to be retrieved as a three-part name: the local name, the\\n namespace prefix, and the namespace URI. Applications should avoid \\nattaching any significance to the choice of prefix, but the information \\nis provided because it can be helpful to human readers. Names are \\nconsidered equal if the namespace URI and local name match.\\n</p><p>In addition, most models provide some way of determining which \\nnamespaces have been declared for a given element. This information is \\nneeded because some XML vocabularies allow qualified names (containing \\nnamespace prefixes) to appear in the content of elements or attributes, \\nas well as in their names. There are three main ways this information \\ncan be provided:\\n</p>\\n<ul><li>As attribute nodes named "xmlns" or "xmlns:xxx", exactly as the \\nnamespaces are written in the source XML document. This is the model \\npresented by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Document_Object_Model" title="Document Object Model">DOM</a>.</li>\\n<li>As namespace declarations: distinguished from attributes, but \\ncorresponding one-to-one with the relevant attributes in the source XML \\ndocument. This is the model presented by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JDOM" title="JDOM">JDOM</a>.</li>\\n<li>As in-scope namespace bindings: in this model, the application is \\nable to determine which namespaces are in scope for any given element, \\nbut is not able to determine which elements contain the actual \\ndeclarations. This is the model used in <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XPath" title="XPath">XPath</a>, <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XSLT" title="XSLT">XSLT</a>, and <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XQuery" title="XQuery">XQuery</a>.</li></ul>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="See_also">See also</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=4" title="Edit section: See also"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<ul><li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namespace" title="Namespace">Namespace</a></li></ul>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2                   [18, TagBody] <div class="shortdescription nomobile noexcerpt noprint searchaux" style="display:none">Method of providing unique elements and attributes in an XML document</div>\\n<p><b>XML namespaces</b> are used for providing uniquely named <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_element" title="Data element">elements</a> and attributes in an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XML" title="XML">XML</a> document. They are defined in a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web_Consortium" title="World Wide Web Consortium">W3C recommendation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-timelinehistory_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-timelinehistory-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> An XML instance may contain element or attribute names from more than one XML vocabulary. If each vocabulary is given a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namespace" title="Namespace">namespace</a>, the ambiguity between identically named elements or attributes can be resolved.\\n</p><p>A simple example would be to consider an XML instance that \\ncontained references to a customer and an ordered product. Both the \\ncustomer element and the product element could have a child element \\nnamed <b>id</b>. References to the <b>id</b> element would therefore be ambiguous; placing them in different namespaces would remove the ambiguity.\\n</p>\\n<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc">\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespace_names">Namespace names</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: Namespace names"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>A <i>namespace name</i> is a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_identifier" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource identifier">uniform resource identifier</a>\\n (URI). Typically, the URI chosen for the namespace of a given XML \\nvocabulary describes a resource under the control of the author or \\norganization defining the vocabulary, such as a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_locator" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource locator">URL</a>\\n for the author's Web server. However, the namespace specification does \\nnot require nor suggest that the namespace URI be used to retrieve \\ninformation; it is simply treated by an XML parser as a string. For \\nexample, the document at <a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a> itself does not contain any code. It simply describes the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XHTML" title="XHTML">XHTML</a>\\n namespace to human readers. Using a URI (such as \\n"http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml") to identify a namespace, rather than a \\nsimple string (such as "xhtml"), reduces the probability of different \\nnamespaces using duplicate identifiers.\\n</p><p>Although the term <i>namespace URI</i> is widespread, the W3C Recommendation refers to it as the <i>namespace name</i>.\\n The specification is not entirely prescriptive about the precise rules \\nfor namespace names (it does not explicitly say that parsers must reject\\n documents where the namespace name is not a valid <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Resource_Identifier" title="Uniform Resource Identifier">Uniform Resource Identifier</a>),\\n and many XML parsers allow any character string to be used. In version \\n1.1 of the recommendation, the namespace name becomes an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationalized_Resource_Identifier" title="Internationalized Resource Identifier">Internationalized Resource Identifier</a>, which licenses the use of non-ASCII characters that in practice were already accepted by nearly all XML software. The term <i>namespace URI</i> persists, however, not only in popular usage, but also in many other specifications from W3C and elsewhere.\\n</p><p>Following publication of the Namespaces recommendation, there was\\n an intensive debate about how a relative URI should be handled, with \\nsome intensely arguing that it should simply be treated as a character \\nstring, and others arguing with conviction that it should be turned into\\n an absolute URI by resolving it against the base URI of the document.<sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The result of the debate was a ruling from W3C that relative URIs were deprecated.<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>\\n</p><p>The use of URIs taking the form of URLs in the http scheme (such as <i><a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a></i>)\\n is common, despite the absence of any formal relationship with the HTTP\\n protocol. The Namespaces specification does not say what should happen \\nif such a URL is dereferenced (that is, if software attempts to retrieve\\n a document from this location). One convention adopted by some users is\\n to place an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RDDL" class="mw-redirect" title="RDDL">RDDL</a> document at the location.<sup id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In general, however, users should assume that the namespace URI is simply a name, not the address of a document on the Web.\\n</p>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespace_declaration">Namespace declaration</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: Namespace declaration"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>An XML namespace is declared using the reserved XML attribute <code>xmlns</code> or <code>xmlns:<i>prefix</i></code>, the value of which must be a valid <a href="#Namespace_names">namespace name</a>.\\n</p><p>For example, the following declaration maps the "xhtml:" prefix to the XHTML namespace:\\n</p>\\n<pre>xmlns:xhtml="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"</pre>\\n<p>Any element or attribute whose name starts with the prefix "xhtml:" \\nis considered to be in the XHTML namespace, if it or an ancestor has the\\n above namespace declaration.\\n</p><p>It is also possible to declare a default namespace. For example:\\n</p>\\n<pre>xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"</pre>\\n<p>In this case, any element without a namespace prefix is considered to\\n be in the XHTML namespace, if it or an ancestor has the above default \\nnamespace declaration.\\n</p><p>If there is no default namespace declaration in scope, the namespace name has no value.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In that case, an element without an explicit namespace prefix is considered not to be in any namespace.\\n</p><p>Attributes are never subject to the default namespace. An \\nattribute without an explicit namespace prefix is considered not to be \\nin any namespace.\\n</p>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Namespaces_in_APIs_and_XML_object_models">Namespaces in APIs and XML object models</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Namespaces in APIs and XML object models"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<p>Different specifications have taken different approaches on how namespace information is presented to applications.\\n</p><p>Nearly all programming models allow the name of an element or \\nattribute node to be retrieved as a three-part name: the local name, the\\n namespace prefix, and the namespace URI. Applications should avoid \\nattaching any significance to the choice of prefix, but the information \\nis provided because it can be helpful to human readers. Names are \\nconsidered equal if the namespace URI and local name match.\\n</p><p>In addition, most models provide some way of determining which \\nnamespaces have been declared for a given element. This information is \\nneeded because some XML vocabularies allow qualified names (containing \\nnamespace prefixes) to appear in the content of elements or attributes, \\nas well as in their names. There are three main ways this information \\ncan be provided:\\n</p>\\n<ul><li>As attribute nodes named "xmlns" or "xmlns:xxx", exactly as the \\nnamespaces are written in the source XML document. This is the model \\npresented by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Document_Object_Model" title="Document Object Model">DOM</a>.</li>\\n<li>As namespace declarations: distinguished from attributes, but \\ncorresponding one-to-one with the relevant attributes in the source XML \\ndocument. This is the model presented by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JDOM" title="JDOM">JDOM</a>.</li>\\n<li>As in-scope namespace bindings: in this model, the application is \\nable to determine which namespaces are in scope for any given element, \\nbut is not able to determine which elements contain the actual \\ndeclarations. This is the model used in <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XPath" title="XPath">XPath</a>, <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XSLT" title="XSLT">XSLT</a>, and <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XQuery" title="XQuery">XQuery</a>.</li></ul>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="See_also">See also</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=XML_namespace&amp;action=edit&amp;section=4" title="Edit section: See also"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>\\n<ul><li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namespace" title="Namespace">Namespace</a></li></ul>\\n<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2                    [19, Tag] <p><b>XML namespaces</b> are used for providing uniquely named <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_element" title="Data element">elements</a> and attributes in an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XML" title="XML">XML</a> document. They are defined in a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web_Consortium" title="World Wide Web Consortium">W3C recommendation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-timelinehistory_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-timelinehistory-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> An XML instance may contain element or attribute names from more than one XML vocabulary. If each vocabulary is given a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namespace" title="Namespace">namespace</a>, the ambiguity between identically named elements or attributes can be resolved.\\n</p>

                    [20, TagBody] <b>XML namespaces</b> are used for providing uniquely named <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_element" title="Data element">elements</a> and attributes in an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XML" title="XML">XML</a> document. They are defined in a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web_Consortium" title="World Wide Web Consortium">W3C recommendation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-timelinehistory_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-timelinehistory-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> An XML instance may contain element or attribute names from more than one XML vocabulary.                    [19, Tag] <p>A <i>namespace name</i> is a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_identifier" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource identifier">uniform resource identifier</a>\\n (URI). Typically, the URI chosen for the namespace of a given XML \\nvocabulary describes a resource under the control of the author or \\norganization defining the vocabulary, such as a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_locator" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource locator">URL</a>\\n for the author's Web server. However, the namespace specification does \\nnot require nor suggest that the namespace URI be used to retrieve \\ninformation; it is simply treated by an XML parser as a string. For \\nexample, the document at <a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a> itself does not contain any code. It simply describes the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XHTML" title="XHTML">XHTML</a>\\n namespace to human readers. Using a URI (such as \\n"http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml") to identify a namespace, rather than a \\nsimple string (such as "xhtml"), reduces the probability of different \\nnamespaces using duplicate identifiers.\\n</p>
                    [20, TagHead] <p>
                     [21, TagName] p
                      [22, Name] p
                    [20, TagBody] A <i>namespace name</i> is a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_identifier" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource identifier">uniform resource identifier</a>\\n (URI). Typically, the URI chosen for the namespace of a given XML \\nvocabulary describes a resource under the control of the author or \\norganization defining the vocabulary, such as a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_resource_locator" class="mw-redirect" title="Uniform resource locator">URL</a>\\n for the author's Web server. However, the namespace specification does \\nnot require nor suggest that the namespace URI be used to retrieve \\ninformation; it is simply treated by an XML parser as a string. For \\nexample, the document at <a rel="nofollow" class="external free" href="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml</a> itself does not contain any code. It simply describes the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XHTML" title="XHTML">XHTML</a>\\n namespace to human readers. Using a URI (such as \\n"http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml") to identify a namespace, rather than a \\nsimple string (such as "xhtml"), reduces the probability of different \\nnamespaces using duplicate identifiers.

                   [19, Tag] <p>Although the term <i>namespace URI</i> is widespread, the W3C Recommendation refers to it as the <i>namespace name</i>.\\n The specification is not entirely prescriptive about the precise rules \\nfor namespace names (it does not explicitly say that parsers must reject\\n documents where the namespace name is not a valid <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Resource_Identifier" title="Uniform Resource Identifier">Uniform Resource Identifier</a>),\\n and many XML parsers allow any character string to be used.
